new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is (tentatively) tonal — 'It seems clear that tone is phonemic' (p. 21) — and 'stress is dependent on tone (and vowel quality)' (p. 20). Word stress, where present, is sonority-driven inside a right-edge three-syllable window: the final syllable is extrametrical; primary stress goes to a penultimate /a/, failing that an antepenultimate /a/, failing that a penultimate then antepenultimate /ɛ/. If no non-final /a/ or /ɛ/ exists the word has no stress; all monosyllables and disyllables are stressless (a degenerate foot is disallowed), as are words whose pitch pattern clashes with stress (falling pitch on a weak syllable, stress on the second of two high syllables, all-low words incl. most loans). Words with a penultimate falling pitch are stressed on that syllable regardless of vowel. Vowel reduction in metrically weak syllables is the diagnostic for stress. Examples: agoˈsaba 'grass', ˈakola 'fire pit', faˈlakɛ 'single man', leˈglɛsi 'wall'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Feet are built around the primary-stressed syllable, iambic or trochaic as needed to foot the most syllables; secondary stress on the non-adjacent foot head, e.g. walugaluju 'mouth harp' -> (ˌwalu)(ˈgalu)ju (p. 23); tobali-afɛ 'five times' [to²ˈba⁴li¹ˌa¹fɛ¹] (p. 24).
new_statements.exceptions: Majority of words stressless (all mono- and disyllables; words lacking non-final /a/ or /ɛ/, e.g. hoklifa 'ant', tetekei 'sweet potato'; words with disallowed stress-tone combinations; all-low-pitch words incl. most Tok Pisin/English loans). Words with penultimate falling pitch are stressed there irrespective of vowel (ɛˈniːno 'tooth', aˈmeːgi 'tongs'); compounds and multimorphemic words 'complex and unpredictable' (p. 24). Author flags open questions: stress-tone combinations, compound stress, stress in inflected verbs/auxiliaries (p. 25). Footnote 9: no evidence that syllable weight influences placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, based mainly on nouns elicited in the frame 'ɛbe X' ('this is an X') on 1984-2000 tape recordings; the author never did fieldwork and calls the whole prosodic analysis tentative ('seems'). Sonority-driven vowel-quality stress in a tonal language; the language of the analysis could equally be filed as weight-sensitive (vowel-quality sonority) — the 'tone language with a stress statement' reading is chosen because the source itself makes tone primary and stress dependent on it.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes the Yale language proper (Yadë/Yalë, formerly 'Nagatman'; ISO nce, glottocode yale1246) of the Yale villages, Sandaun Province, PNG; no dialects are distinguished. Data are the Campbells' 1984-2015 archived recordings and notes, reanalysed by Aannestad without fieldwork, so the prosodic description is explicitly tentative.

new_statements.quote: Stress often falls on the penultimate syllable of mono-morphemic words. This is the most common type of stress placement. The greatest majority of two syllable words are stressed on the penultimate syllable. Three or more syllable words have more variation. They are often stressed on the penultimate but they can also be stressed on the antepenultimate syllable. We think stress in Yale is assigned in the lexicon and not purely assigned by rules. In the following examples stress appears to be contrastive. But other factors such as syllable timing may also be affecting stress.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Yale has an empty rule; the only existing statement (Aannestad, Campbell & Campbell 2020, §2.4.2) reads the language as tonal with sonority-driven stress: final syllable extrametrical, primary stress on a penultimate /a/, else antepenultimate /a/, else /ɛ/ in the same order; all monosyllables and disyllables and 'the majority of Yale words' stressless; stress dependent on tone and vowel quality. The 2001 OPD differs in type: stress is 'assigned in the lexicon', 'appears to be contrastive', and disyllables are overwhelmingly penult-stressed (2020: all disyllables stressless); tone is not mentioned at all. The two agree only that stress, when present, sits in the penult…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexically assigned rather than rule-governed, but with a strong default: penultimate in monomorphemic words (nearly all disyllables are penult-stressed); words of three or more syllables are usually penult-stressed but may be antepenult-stressed. Stress 'appears to be contrastive' (five minimal pairs, p. 3: 'so.lo 'fish net' vs so.'lo 'sip'; 'no.e 'bird sp.' vs no.'e 'male name'; 'te.le 'village name' vs he.'le 'white ant'; 'jo.wa 'one' vs jo.'wa 'without'; a.'fo.lo 'short' vs 'a.fu.lu 'knead'), though the authors suspect syllable timing contributes: the apparently final-stressed members have a very short (underlined) syllable, and they propose that very short syllables do not count for stress placement, so 1b-4b are effectively monosyllables and 5b a disyllable. Nothing is said about tone despite the heading.
new_statements.exceptions: 'There are few examples of stress on the ultimate syllable and the majority of these words have very short syllables. We suggest that very short syllables are not counted in the stress placement' (p. 3). Antepenultimate stress in some 3+-syllable words. Syllable shortening 'from almost no change in length to times when the affected syllable becomes so short that the vowel is barely perceived' (pp. 3-4). The 'Conventions: Phonological' section (p. 4) adds: 'A high vowel becomes mid-centralized before a syllable with primary stress unless the consonant in the stressed syllable has the same point of articulation.'
new_statements.identity_note: All three listed works and the 2020 grammar describe the same language, Yale (also Yadë, Nagatman; ISO nce), Sandaun Province, PNG, population c. 600 (1990 census), villages Nagatiman, Hela, Dila (OPD 2001 header). The OPD gives no dialect; a 1995 'Dialect Survey of the Yale (Nagatman, Yade) Language' by the Campbells is cited in its bibliography but not located online.

new_statements.quote: [p. 2] A plural suffix -rë or -re is added on to certain nouns to indicate plurality. The stress is shifted to remain on the penultimate syllable when the plural suffix is added. The pluralized form is one phonological unit. 1) ˈnëba 'child' nëˈba-re 'children' 2) ˈama 'dog' aˈma-re 'dogs' 3) ˈdife 'village' diˈfe-rë 'villages' [p. 32] When two nouns are joined together, the stress patterns are altered and stress shifts one syllable to the right on the compound noun stem. 161) ˈtobo + ˈti ... toˈboti [p. 33] 163) ˈnëba + ˈmusu = nëˈbamusu ... 165) ˈmise + ˈnëba = miˈsenëba ... Sometimes the stress pattern remains on the first syllable of the first word of the compound stem. These words all have to do with people.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (world-r2-2026-09-17) carries no rule, and the only existing statement (Aannestad, Campbell & Campbell 2020 §2.4.2) was read as 'unclear or contradictory' (sonority-driven: stress a penultimate /a/, else antepenultimate /a/, else /ɛ/, final syllable extrametrical, many words stressless). The 1987 ms supplies an explicit placement — penultimate, maintained under suffixation, with a one-syllable rightward shift in compounds — which matches the Campbells' own 2001 Organised Phonology Data already held by the project ('Stress often falls on the penultimate syllable of mono-morphemic words.. the most common type of stress placement'; lexically assigned, apparent contrasts attr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No dedicated stress section (this is a grammar sketch), but stress is marked on cited forms and two morphological statements fix its position: disyllabic nouns carry initial (= penultimate) stress, and when the plural suffix -re/-rë is added stress moves rightward so that it stays on the penultimate syllable of the suffixed word (ˈnëba > nëˈba-re), the plural form counting as one phonological word. In noun-noun compounds stress shifts one syllable to the right of the first member's stressed syllable (ˈtobo+ˈti > toˈboti, ˈmaba+ti > maˈbati; in four-syllable compounds this lands on the antepenult: nëˈbamusu, miˈsenëba), i.e. a single word stress near the right edge with penultimate as the stated target.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said; compounds are described as having a single (shifted) stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds denoting people keep stress on the first syllable of the first member (ˈoneho 'people', ˈmisenaho 'married man', ˈhonamise 'married woman', ˈmiseho 'brother-in-law'); the authors found no non-human examples of this pattern. Some nouns have suppletive plurals (mise/one) to which the stress statement does not apply.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1987 ms calls the language Yadë (Nagatman, Nagatiman), c. 580 speakers in eight villages of West Sepik Province between Amanab and Edwaki, and states 'There are no known dialects'; data collected monolingually in Nagatiman village from May 1984. Same variety as the 2001 OPD and the 2020 grammar (which reuse the Campbells' Nagatiman data).

readall_conflicts: The two primary descriptions disagree on the type of the stress system. Campbell & Campbell 2001 (OPD, p. 3) say stress is lexically assigned, mostly penultimate (nearly all disyllables penult-stressed, longer words penult or antepenult), 'appears to be contrastive' on five minimal pairs, with very short syllables not counted, and say nothing about tone. Aannestad, Campbell & Campbell 2020 (§2.4, pp. 20-25, the existing statement) treat Yale as tonal ('It seems clear that tone is phonemic', p. 21), make stress dependent on tone and vowel sonority (penultimate /a/, else antepenultimate /a/, else /ɛ/, final syllable extrametrical), and state that all monosyllables and disyllables and the majority of words are stressless, with stress diagnosed by vowel reduction. They agree only that stress, where present, falls on the penult or antepenult and is not fully rule-predictable. Both are explicitly tentative ('We think', 'seems to be'), and both derive from the Campbells' field data; the 2020 grammar, co-authored by the Campbells, is the later and fuller analysis, so it is taken as the better-supported reading, but the 2001 lexical/contrastive claim is not retracted anywhere I could read. The 1987 grammar and the 1992 OPD could not be opened, so whether they add a third position is unknown.
